overview: Troodon formosus was a small Late Cretaceous coelurosaur from North America with unusually large brain-to-body ratio, large forward-facing eyes suggesting binocular vision, and sickle-shaped second toe claws. These features led Dale Russell's famous 1982 thought experiment imagining a "dinosauroid" — what Troodon might have evolved into had it survived — a humanoid figure with a large brain and bipedal stance.

Troodon is now a complicated taxon: much material historically referred to it may belong to different animals, and recent analyses suggest the name may apply only to isolated teeth, with the skeletal material belonging to Stenonychosaurus. Regardless of nomenclature, troodontids represent the most neurologically sophisticated non-avian dinosaurs documented from the fossil record.

fossilSites.name: Judith River Formation
fossilSites.note: Late Campanian deposits with Troodon teeth and skeletal material; associated with the first known dinosaur eggs attributed to troodontids.

fossilSites.name: Two Medicine Formation
fossilSites.note: Campanian beds with Troodon nesting sites — embryos and eggs, including evidence of partial incubation by brooding adults.

articles.title: Intelligence and senses
articles.body: The endocranial volume of troodontids is the largest relative to body size of any non-avian dinosaur group. The large orbits suggest good vision; the orbit orientation implies some degree of binocular overlap — useful for judging distance when hunting. The ears show adaptations for detecting low-frequency sounds. Together these features imply a predator capable of complex sensory integration.

articles.title: Nesting behaviour
articles.body: Troodontid nests are known from the Two Medicine Formation, where eggs were laid in pairs (consistent with two functional oviducts) in large clutches arranged in a ring. Adult specimens found in brooding posture over nests suggest parental care, one of the most direct lines of evidence for this behaviour in non-avian dinosaurs.

articles.title: Taxonomy
articles.body: The Troodon name has been applied to a great range of material from multiple formations. Recent taxonomic work restricts Troodon formosus to tooth material from the Judith River Formation, while skeletal material from other sites may represent distinct species or genera. This instability makes "Troodon" a moving target in North American Late Cretaceous ecology.

fossilRecord.formations: Historically Dinosaur Park Formation and other Late Cretaceous North American material
fossilRecord.material: Historically based on teeth; much referred material has been reassessed.
fossilRecord.paleo: Late Cretaceous North American records, but the genus is now treated cautiously.
fossilRecord.evidence: Dental and partial skeletal evidence once grouped under Troodon has been split or reinterpreted in recent research.

record.mya: Campanian, about 77-74 million years ago for the currently argued species concept
record.taxonomicStatus: contested tooth-based name; a 2025 paper defended validity and proposed a neotype, reversing the prevalent post-2017 treatment
record.description: Troodon formosus was named from a single tooth collected in Montana. From 2017 the tooth was widely treated as insufficient to anchor the many skeletons historically assigned to Troodon, and those fossils were reassigned to Stenonychosaurus and other taxa. A 2025 study defended Troodon as valid, synonymised Stenonychosaurus with it and proposed a Two Medicine Formation skeleton as a neotype. That neotype requires ICZN action, so the issue is not presented as settled.
facts: The holotype ANSP 9259 is one isolated tooth with incomplete locality information.
The familiar full-body reconstruction was assembled from referred troodontid skeletons, not from the holotype.
The 2017 revisions treated Troodon as a doubtful name and restored Stenonychosaurus for Dinosaur Park material.
The 2025 paper argued for priority and stability under Troodon and proposed MOR 553 as a neotype, but explicitly noted that only the ICZN can replace an existing holotype in this way.

presentation.heroLead: A famous name resting on a single Cretaceous tooth: whether the big-brained, sickle-clawed troodontid skeletons of Montana and Alberta should be called Troodon is an open dispute.

heroMedia.title: Life restoration of a Troodon-like troodontid
heroMedia.alt: Life restoration of a feathered, long-legged troodontid theropod with large eyes and a raised sickle claw on each foot, in side view
heroMedia.caption: Restoration of the North American troodontid usually pictured as Troodon. The body plan comes from referred skeletons, some now called Stenonychosaurus; the name-bearing fossil is a single tooth, and the feathers and colour are interpretive.

animalParagraphs: Troodon was named by Joseph Leidy in 1856 for one small, coarsely serrated tooth from the Judith River beds of Montana, one of the first dinosaurs named from North America. For over a century the tooth was compared with lizards and then with plant-eating dinosaurs before being recognised as belonging to a small theropod.

The animal most people picture as Troodon is a lightly built, long-legged troodontid about two to three metres long, with very large eyes, one of the largest brains relative to body size among dinosaurs, and a raised sickle claw on each foot. Those features are documented in skeletons from Alberta and Montana, including nesting sites with eggs and embryos, that were referred to Troodon during the late twentieth century.

Since 2017 many researchers have argued that a single tooth cannot be distinguished from those of related troodontids, and have restored the name Stenonychosaurus for the Alberta skeletons. A 2025 study reversed course, defending Troodon and proposing a Two Medicine Formation skeleton as a replacement type, but that change needs a ruling from the zoological naming commission before it takes effect.
animalHighlights: The name-bearing fossil is one tooth, ANSP 9259, with only approximate locality information.
Referred skeletons describe a large-eyed, large-brained troodontid with a sickle claw, and nests with eggs and embryos have been linked to the same animal.
Whether those skeletons can carry the name Troodon is actively disputed between the 2017 and 2025 revisions.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: Coarse serrations and relatively small, leaf-shaped teeth differ from typical meat-eaters and have been read as a mixed diet. No gut contents are known for the holotype or referred skeletons.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Long hindlimbs indicate a fast two-legged animal, but every limb bone belongs to referred troodontid material whose link to the name is contested.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: The holotype tooth gives no size directly. Length comes from referred skeletons that may or may not be the same species.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: No skin or feather impressions are known from any North American troodontid; the feathered restoration rests on Asian relatives.

whereFacts.label: Rock unit
whereFacts.value: Judith River Formation; referred material from the Two Medicine and Dinosaur Park formations

whereFacts.label: Type locality
whereFacts.value: Judith River badlands, Montana, USA, exact site unknown

locality.name: Judith River badlands
locality.note: The holotype tooth was collected in 1855 with only general locality data. The proposed neotype comes from the Two Medicine Formation near Choteau, Montana.

presentation.classificationSummary: Troodon is the name-giving genus of Troodontidae, a family of small, bird-like theropods within Paraves. The family is well defined; the problem is that the tooth on which the genus rests may not be diagnostic below the family level.

related.reason: The name restored for the Alberta skeletons that were long called Troodon.
Compare with a Mongolian troodontid known from a skull and partial skeleton.
Compare with an early Chinese troodontid that shows the origins of the group.

questions.title: Can one tooth define a species?
questions.copy: Troodontid teeth are distinctive as a family, but distinguishing genera from teeth alone is difficult. The 2017 revisions concluded the holotype was undiagnostic; the 2025 study argued it can be matched to skeletons.

questions.title: Will the neotype be accepted?
questions.copy: Replacing an existing holotype requires an application to the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature. Until a ruling exists, MOR 553 is a proposal rather than the type.

questions.title: Whose nests are they?
questions.copy: Eggs, embryos and clutches from the Two Medicine Formation have been assigned to Troodon. If the name is restricted to the tooth, the nesting evidence belongs to a troodontid whose name depends on the outcome of the dispute.

review.ageReviewNote: A single genus-wide 77-66 Ma range is not defensible while the name-bearing tooth and referred skeletons remain taxonomically disputed. The current 2025 species concept focuses on Campanian Montana and Alberta material.

sources.citation: van der Reest & Currie (2017), Troodontids from the Dinosaur Park Formation and implications for deinonychosaur diversity
Varricchio, Hogan & Gardner (2025), validity of Troodon formosus

residualUncertainty: The proposed neotype has not yet been established by an ICZN ruling.
Researchers disagree on whether the original tooth can anchor the expanded skeletal species concept.
Historic records from many formations cannot all be retained without specimen-level revision.

evidence.summary: The name is based on one tooth; a 2025 attempt to reconnect it to skeletal material has reopened rather than eliminated the taxonomic dispute.
evidence.material: Single tooth holotype; more complete skeletons belong to a contested referred species concept and proposed neotype.
evidence.formations: Judith River locality uncertain; proposed neotype from Two Medicine Formation, Montana; compared material from Dinosaur Park Formation, Alberta.
evidence.confidenceLimit: Troodontid anatomy is known from the referred specimens, but the name Troodon is not yet securely anchored to them.
evidence.sourceBasis: 2017 Dinosaur Park revision and Varricchio et al. 2025 neotype proposal.

specimens.name: Holotype
specimens.institution: Academy of Natural Sciences of Drexel University, Philadelphia
specimens.note: Single tooth from the Judith River beds of Montana, named by Leidy in 1856; the only secure name-bearing fossil.

specimens.name: Proposed neotype
specimens.note: Partial skeleton from the Two Medicine Formation proposed in 2025 as a replacement type; pending an ICZN ruling.

panel.headline: One tooth carries the name; the skeletons are disputed.
panel.standfirst: The only fossil securely attached to the name Troodon is the holotype tooth ANSP 9259. The skulls, skeletons, eggs and embryos usually shown under the name are referred troodontid material whose assignment has been reversed twice since 2017.

coverage.label: Low
coverage.basis: Securely name-bearing material is a single tooth. Skeletal coverage would be far higher if the referred Montana and Alberta specimens are accepted, but that referral is the subject of an unresolved dispute.

metrics.label: Key limitation
metrics.value: Name not anchored to a skeleton

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: The holotype is a single tooth crown about a centimetre tall with large, hooked serrations. Referred material, if accepted, includes partial skulls, braincases, limb bones and vertebrae from the Dinosaur Park and Two Medicine formations, together with nests, eggs and embryonic bones.
knownRemains.note: Everything beyond the tooth depends on a taxonomic argument. The panel treats the tooth as the secure evidence and the rest as provisionally referred.

media.title: Holotype tooth ANSP 9259 in three views
media.alt: Three magnified photographs of the small serrated Troodon formosus holotype tooth showing its side, wear facet and front
media.caption: The holotype tooth photographed at six times life size for Loris Russell's 1948 review, showing the coarse serrations and a wear facet. This tooth is the entire secure basis of the name.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Secure: one isolated tooth. Referred: partial skulls, braincases and jaws from Alberta and Montana troodontids whose generic name is disputed.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Secure: none. Referred: vertebrae from partial skeletons such as MOR 553 in the Two Medicine Formation.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Secure: none. Referred: hindlimb, pelvic and forelimb material including the sickle-clawed foot known from Dinosaur Park Formation specimens.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Nests, eggs and embryos from the Two Medicine Formation are attributed to the same troodontid. No skin, feather or gut-content evidence is known.

specimenCards.title: ANSP 9259 · holotype
specimenCards.description: A single tooth collected by Ferdinand Hayden in 1855 from the Judith River beds and named by Joseph Leidy in 1856. It remains the only fossil that unquestionably belongs to Troodon formosus.
specimenCards.meta: Judith River Formation, Montana · Academy of Natural Sciences of Drexel University, Philadelphia

specimenCards.title: MOR 553 · Two Medicine Formation skeleton
specimenCards.description: A partial skeleton from Montana put forward in 2025 as a replacement type to tie the name to skeletal anatomy and to sink Stenonychosaurus into Troodon. The proposal is not in force until the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature rules on it.
specimenCards.meta: Two Medicine Formation, Montana · Museum of the Rockies, Bozeman · status pending

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: One serrated tooth with a wear facet. Referred skeletons, nests and embryos exist but are attached to the name by argument, not by overlap with the holotype.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: The tooth is troodontid. The 2017 revisions judged it undiagnostic below family level; the 2025 study argued it matches Two Medicine and Dinosaur Park skeletons and that Troodon has priority over Stenonychosaurus.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Whether the neotype will be accepted, whether the tooth and skeletons are one species, and how many historic Troodon records from other formations survive specimen-level revision.

panel.limitations: The coverage band describes the material securely attached to the name at genus level. It is an editorial evidence summary, not a published percentage and not a count of PBDB occurrences, and it will change if the proposed neotype is ratified.
